briefs.working_title: How to earn links in India without buying a single one
briefs.angle: Practical. Trade association listings, supplier and partner pages, local press and trade publications, founder commentary on data journalists' requests, and genuinely useful tools or datasets. Be blunt about paid guest post networks and what happens when they get deindexed.

selling to us clients from india

briefs.working_title: The LinkedIn posts that get Indian B2B founders into buying conversations

briefs.working_title: How coaching centres get admissions from search instead of from hoardings

how to find low competition keywords

briefs.working_title: Chennai's manufacturers are invisible online, and their buyers are searching anyway
briefs.angle: City and sector specific. Manufacturing and auto ancillary firms rely on relationships and IndiaMART while procurement teams search technical specifications. Show the query types and what a product or capability page needs to contain.

briefs.angle: City specific opinion. Pune's mix of IT services, manufacturing and education needs different marketing from Mumbai's consumer heavy market, and the imported playbook fails. Say what to look for locally instead.

briefs.angle: City specific and respectful. Decades of relationship led trade, now a generation of buyers who search first. What the transition looks like, what to do first, and why the answer is not a rebrand.

lead generation for small business india

briefs.angle: Practical. Calculators, benchmarks, templates, teardowns and audits work. Generic ebooks do not. Give five specific examples per business type and the follow up sequence that has to exist behind them.

briefs.angle: Analysis for fintech and healthcare. YMYL means Google holds the content to a higher evidence bar, and RBI and advertising rules hold you to a legal one. Show how to build authority signals inside those limits.

briefs.angle: Practical. Most Indian stores optimise product pages and leave category pages empty. Cover category copy, faceted navigation and index bloat, out of stock handling, product schema and reviews.

briefs.angle: Practical and slightly contrarian. Most small Indian businesses run sales out of personal WhatsApp and lose track. Cover the minimum viable system, when a real CRM earns its cost, and the follow up cadence that recovers dead leads.

briefs.angle: Opinion with an exercise. Everyone serving everyone competes on price. Walk through narrowing until it feels uncomfortable, with real before and after examples of a service business rewriting its homepage line.

briefs.working_title: Short video is where Indian buyers research now, and search still indexes it
briefs.angle: Practical. Which businesses should bother, the format that works for a service business, titles and descriptions that get found in search, and repurposing one shoot across Reels, Shorts and the site.

secondary_keywords: can i use google analytics on a medical website

briefs.working_title: Why your third location ranks and your other four do not
briefs.angle: Practical. Location pages that are the same page with the city swapped get treated as thin duplicates. Cover the separate Google Business Profile per location, distinct staff, hours, photos and embedded directions, the internal linking pattern from a location index, and the difference between a storefront and a service area business in how you handle the address. secondary_keywords: how to get more google reviews

Cover Yelp's review recommendation filter and why soliciting reviews backfires there, when paid Yelp genuinely works (restaurants, home services in dense metros), and how to decide with a simple cost per call comparison. Give the numbers to pull before renewing a Yelp contract.

briefs.primary_keyword: how much should i spend on google ads

briefs.angle: Practical arithmetic. Start from lifetime value and close rate, work backwards to an allowable cost per lead, then to a daily budget that can actually gather enough conversions for smart bidding to learn. Explain the learning threshold problem, why a budget too small to produce conversions weekly is money set on fire, and the honest answer that some markets are too expensive to enter at the budget available. Include the full calculation in dollars.

briefs.working_title: Everyone bought an AI SDR and the inbox got worse for all of us
briefs.angle: Opinion piece on outbound saturation. AI made it trivial to send personalised looking email at volume, which destroyed the signal that personalisation used to carry, and reply rates fell for everyone including the people who were doing it properly. Argue the winners now go the other way: fewer, genuinely researched, harder to fake touches. Rubbish the practice and not the vendors. End on what actually still gets replies.

secondary_keywords: how to ask for reviews legally

briefs.angle: Opinion and compliance. The FTC rule on fake and manipulated reviews put real penalties behind buying reviews, incentivising only positive ones and suppressing negatives. Argue that this is good news for the operator who never cheated, because the gap closes. Cover review gating specifically, since plenty of reputable software still nudges people towards it, and give the compliant way to ask that works better anyway.
briefs.audience: Local business owners and marketing managers

secondary_keywords: how to market on reddit without getting banned

Argue the only version that works is participation under a real name over months, and that every agency selling Reddit seeding is burning an asset. Cover what moderators actually ban, and the one legitimate way a business account adds value.

briefs.working_title: Corporate builds the campaign, the franchisee ignores it, and both sides are right

Corporate optimises for brand consistency and national scale, the franchisee optimises for the phone ringing this week in one zip code, and the ad fund sits in the middle satisfying neither. Argue for a split: corporate owns brand and the asset library, the operator owns local and gets real latitude. Be concrete about which channels belong on which side of that line.

briefs.working_title: Estonia has 1.3 million people, so your SEO plan should barely mention Estonia
briefs.angle: Practical international SEO. Domestic search volume is tiny, so the growth is in Finnish, Swedish, German and English language demand. Cover choosing between subfolders and country domains, hreflang done properly, whether to translate or write natively per market, and how to size demand per country before committing. Give the exact process for validating a market with a small test before building fifty pages.
briefs.audience: Estonian founders selling into the EU and Nordics

briefs.working_title: Your e-Residency company looks fine on paper and suspicious on your website
briefs.angle: Practical trust building. An Estonian OU run remotely is completely legitimate, but a site with no named people, a virtual office address and no proof of work reads as a shell to a cautious EU buyer. Cover the trust signals that matter: named founders with real credentials, a physical presence statement that is honest, VAT number displayed, EU customer references, and clear terms. Give the page by page checklist.
briefs.audience: e-Residents and remote founders of Estonian companies

briefs.working_title: There is not enough search volume in Estonia to run the campaign you planned
briefs.angle: Practical. Smart bidding needs a conversion volume that a 1.3 million person market often cannot supply, so campaigns sit in learning forever. Cover consolidating campaigns rather than splitting them, running EU wide or Nordic wide with language targeting instead of country by country, using broader match with tight negatives because exact match starves, and when to accept manual bidding. Give the volume threshold to check before choosing a bid strategy.

briefs.working_title: Running your site in Estonian and English without splitting your own rankings
briefs.angle: Practical technical SEO. Bilingual sites usually go wrong in three ways: no hreflang, hreflang without return tags, and an automatic language redirect that stops crawlers seeing either version. Cover the correct annotation including x-default, why a language switcher must be a real link, and how to decide which content genuinely needs both languages rather than translating everything by reflex. Give the exact tag block to copy.

briefs.working_title: Selling into Finland and Sweden from Tallinn, without the pitch that works at home
briefs.angle: Practical market entry. Nordic B2B buying is consensus driven, slower and allergic to pressure, so an outbound sequence tuned for urgency actively backfires. Cover LinkedIn as the primary channel, the GDPR position on cold B2B email in the Nordics, localising proof rather than copy, and pricing presentation in euro versus krona. Give a sequence outline that respects a longer buying cycle.
briefs.audience: Estonian B2B founders and sales leads

briefs.working_title: Nobody buys your software because Estonia is a digital nation
briefs.angle: Blunt opinion on positioning. The e-Estonia story is a genuine national achievement and a weak commercial differentiator, because it says nothing about whether this product solves the buyer's problem. Argue that country of origin is at best a tiebreaker and at worst a substitute for having a point of view. Give the replacement: a specific claim about outcome that a competitor could not copy onto their own homepage.

briefs.working_title: EU data residency stopped being a compliance cost and started being a reason to switch
briefs.angle: Analysis and opinion. European buyers are increasingly nervous about US hosted data, which turns GDPR compliance and EU hosting from an expense into a live sales argument for a European vendor. Argue for putting it on the pricing page rather than burying it in a trust centre, while warning against the lazy version that just shouts privacy without specifics. Cover what buyers actually ask for in procurement.

secondary_keywords: what small companies can copy from unicorns
briefs.working_title: Most of what the Estonian unicorns did is useless to a company of nine people
briefs.angle: Opinion and analysis. Founders copy the tactics of companies that had capital, headcount and a category already forming, then wonder why the same moves do nothing. Separate what genuinely transfers at small scale from what requires a war chest. Argue that the transferable part is almost always narrow focus and obsessive customer contact, not brand campaigns. Do not disparage the companies, criticise the copying.

briefs.working_title: What actually needs fixing in Shopify SEO
briefs.angle: Practical, Shopify specific. The platform's own constraints are the story: duplicate product URLs under /collections/, thin collection pages, the theme's default title templates, and faceted navigation generating crawl waste. Argue that product and collection pages are the money pages and most stores put all their effort into the blog instead. Give the settings path for each fix and say plainly which of the popular SEO apps solve a real problem and which sell a report.
briefs.audience: Shopify store owners and ecommerce managers

secondary_keywords: why do my numbers not match
briefs.working_title: Why GA4 and Google Ads report different numbers
briefs.angle: Practical reconciliation. Explain the four real causes: different attribution models, different conversion windows, modelled and consent gap conversions, and session versus event based counting. Then the rule that matters, which is that you pick one source per decision rather than trying to make them agree. Give the three reports to compare and the decision each one is allowed to drive. Be clear that a permanent gap is normal and only a widening gap is a signal.

briefs.primary_keyword: klaviyo email flows that make money

briefs.angle: Practical and specific. Welcome, browse abandonment, checkout abandonment and post purchase carry nearly all automated revenue for most stores. For each: what the emails should say, the timing, and the single metric that tells you it is working. Then the deliverability floor underneath all of it, since a beautifully built flow landing in the promotions tab earns nothing. Tie back to the domain authentication work in the cold email posts rather than repeating it.

secondary_keywords: how to get more customers home services

secondary_keywords: how to get more dental patients

Not legal or medical advice, tell them to check with their own counsel.
briefs.audience: Dental practice owners and office managers

briefs.working_title: Why law firm marketing fails at intake rather than at the ad
briefs.angle: Practical, and the argument is that lead volume is almost never the constraint. Legal is among the most expensive categories in paid search, commonly quoted near ten dollars a click and well over a hundred a lead, so a firm that loses half its enquiries to slow intake is wasting the most expensive traffic on the internet. Cover state bar advertising rules as a real constraint on claims and testimonials, then the intake fixes. Not legal advice, check the rules in your own state.
briefs.audience: Law firm partners and marketing managers

secondary_keywords: how to fire a marketing agency
briefs.working_title: The agency warning signs that look like professionalism
briefs.angle: Opinion, and deliberately narrower than the existing agency posts so it does not repeat them. Focus only on the signals visible before you sign and inside the first sixty days, specifically the ones that read as competence: the polished plan produced before any access to your data, the report that only ever contains good news, the account opened in the agency's own name, and the proposal that answers a question you did not ask. Criticise practices and structures, never a named firm.

briefs.primary_keyword: hubspot vs salesforce for small business
briefs.working_title: Which CRM should a small business actually choose
briefs.angle: Comparison, and be scrupulously fair to both since the playbook forbids rubbishing named companies. State the ranking basis in the post. The real argument is that the feature comparison is the wrong axis: most small companies buy a system nobody in the building can administer, and the deciding question is who maintains it on a Tuesday afternoon. Cover what each is genuinely strong at, the cost that arrives later rather than at signature, and when the honest answer is a spreadsheet for another year.

briefs.working_title: Most demand generation is demand capture with a new name
briefs.angle: Analysis with a clear position. Genuine demand creation makes somebody want a category they were not shopping for. Nearly everything sold as demand generation is capture: bidding on existing intent and taking credit for it. Argue that the distinction decides your whole measurement approach, because capture is attributable and creation is not, and teams keep killing creation work for failing an attribution test it was never going to pass. Use the buying group and pipeline sourced shift as the evidence.

briefs.primary_keyword: remote marketing consultant vs local agency los angeles
secondary_keywords: local agency vs freelancer los angeles
briefs.working_title: Does a Los Angeles business need a Los Angeles agency?
briefs.angle: Opinion, built entirely on what makes LA different. The metro sprawls across 88 separate cities, so being physically nearby tells you nothing about knowing your customers, and proximity is close to a worthless signal here. The two things a genuinely local partner does provide are Spanish language creative that is written rather than translated, and knowing which of those 88 cities your buyers actually live in, which is a radius targeting skill. Everything else travels fine over a video call.
briefs._local_specifics: Entertainment and DTC ecommerce dominate. Enormous Spanish speaking market, so English-only campaigns leave money on the table. The metro sprawls across 88 cities, which makes proximity a weak signal and radius targeting a real skill.

briefs.primary_keyword: remote marketing consultant vs local agency manhattan
secondary_keywords: local agency vs freelancer new york
briefs.working_title: In Manhattan the question is not local or remote, it is agency at all
briefs.angle: Opinion specific to New York County, where roughly 130,000 people work in marketing and advertising and most serious buyers already have in-house teams. So the real decision is not which agency but whether you need one rather than one more senior hire, and Manhattan salary levels change that arithmetic in a way they do not elsewhere. Argue that the genuine opening for outside help here is filling a named specialist gap rather than full service, and that local price anchoring is the highest in the country.
briefs._local_specifics: Roughly 130,000 marketing and advertising employees, the largest concentration in the country. Most serious buyers have in-house teams, so the opening is specialist gap-filling, not full service. Price anchoring is the highest in the US.

briefs.primary_keyword: remote marketing consultant vs local agency san jose
secondary_keywords: local agency vs freelancer san jose
briefs.working_title: Hiring marketing help when your buyers will audit the method
briefs.angle: Opinion for Santa Clara County, where product led growth is the default assumption and a lot of companies are structurally sceptical of agencies for reasons that are partly earned. Argue that the winnable outside work here is measurement, technical SEO and attribution rather than campaign execution, and that anybody selling into this county has to survive a technical buyer reading their methodology rather than their case studies. Location is irrelevant. Withstanding scrutiny is not.
briefs.audience: Santa Clara County founders and marketing leads
